docs.title: 4.3 Adding a Version
docs.text:
To add a new version:

  1. Select a tool from the dropdown.
  2. Click Add Version.
  3. In the modal form, fill in the version number and release date.

The form also includes two dynamic sections: Changes and Downloads.

For Changes, you can add multiple change entries. Click the + Add change button to create a new input field for each change. Enter a short description such as “Fixed a parsing error” or “Added GPU acceleration support”.

For Downloads, you can add multiple download links. Each download entry contains:

  • Name – the label for the download, such as “Windows 64-bit” or “Linux source”.
  • URL – the download URL.
  • Icon Class – a Font Awesome icon class, such as fab fa-windows or fab fa-linux.

Click Save to store the version.

Figure 7. Add Version. Each change and download is a separate dynamic row; the version number is the user-facing label, not an automatic build counter.

docs.title: 4.4 Editing and Deleting Versions
docs.text:
Each version row in the list has Edit and Delete buttons.

Clicking Edit opens the version modal with the existing changes and downloads pre-filled. You can modify any value, add new entries, or remove existing ones.

Clicking Delete prompts for confirmation and then removes the version record permanently.

docs.title: 5. Frontend Display
docs.text:
The public website displays tools in two places: the Tools listing page and the Tool Detail page.

The tools listing page shows all tools in a card-style layout. Each card includes the tool icon, name, type badge, description, key features, and links to GitHub and the official website. A “View Details” button leads to the tool detail page.

The tool detail page presents the extended information from the Tool Detail management page. It includes a hero section with the tool name and short description, a metadata panel with version, language, license, and update date, the detailed description content, citation information if available, and a version history section with download links.

The frontend loads tool data through the API endpoints. The tool list page fetches data from api/data.php?type=tools, while the tool detail page loads api/data.php?type=tool-detail&name=... and api/data.php?type=tool-versions&name=....

Figure 8. The public Tools page. Cards are rendered from the tool list API and link to the detail page.

Figure 9. The public tool detail page. Metadata, citation, and version downloads are assembled from separate records.

docs.title: 6. Multilingual Considerations
docs.text:
Tool names, descriptions, and version information are stored as raw text in the database. The current core does not translate these fields automatically.

If you need to present tool information in multiple languages, consider one of the following approaches:

  • Keep the tool content in a single primary language, such as English, while the rest of the site interface switches language normally.
  • Use the Dynamic Multi-Language plugin’s filter system to add custom translations for tool fields if needed.
  • Store bilingual text directly in the tool description field, for example by providing both Chinese and English paragraphs separated by headings.

The plugin system provides the tool_list_item filter, which allows developers to modify tool data before it is rendered on the frontend.

docs.title: 7. Operational Checks
docs.text:
• Every tool has a unique name and a valid type.
  • A detail record exists before the public detail link is promoted.
  • Version numbers follow one convention (for example 1.2.0, not a mix of v1.2 and 1.2.0).
  • Each download URL is reachable without an admin session.
  • The tool card and detail page return the same record after a rename.
  • Deleting a tool has been checked against its detail/version rows in a staging database.

If a detail page returns 404 for a tool that exists in the list, check the detail record's identifier and the tool-detail API parameter. If a version is missing, confirm that the selected tool in the dropdown matches the tool that owns the version row.

docs.title: 8. Next Steps
docs.text:
After managing tools, you may want to continue with:

  • Projects – manage research projects and portfolios.
  • Publications – manage academic publications.
  • Slides – manage homepage carousel slides.
  • Research News – manage laboratory news and announcements.
  • Site Settings – configure the homepage sections that display tools and other content.

docs.title: Users Management
docs.text:
This chapter explains how to manage administrator accounts in the LabPress administration panel. The Users module controls who can access the admin area and which parts of the system each user is allowed to manage.

The guide focuses on practical operations: creating users, editing permissions, changing passwords, and removing accounts. It also describes the permission model and provides security recommendations for day-to-day user management.

docs.title: 1. Overview
docs.text:
LabPress uses a simple role-based permission system. Every user account has a username, a password hash, and a list of permissions stored as a JSON array. The permission list determines which admin pages and API endpoints the user can access.

The user management page is available from the admin sidebar under Users. From this page, administrators can add new users, edit existing users, delete accounts, and change passwords.

All user data is stored in the users table. The permission values are stored in JSON format and can include one or more of the following:

  • all – full access to every module and setting.
  • publications – access to publications and news management.
  • slides – access to slides management.
  • tools – access to tool, project, and category management.
  • users – access to user management.

docs.title: 1.1 Authentication and permission flow
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A[Login form] --> B[password_verify against users.password_hash]
    B -->|fail| C[Reject login]
    B -->|success| D[session: user + permissions JSON]
    D --> E[Admin view guard]
    E --> F{hasPermission required key?}
    F -->|all or key| G[Render view]
    F -->|no| H[Permission error]
    D --> I[Public header account entry]
    I --> J[Show permitted admin shortcuts]

The public account menu uses the same $_SESSION['permissions'] array as the admin views. It is a convenience layer, not a separate authorization system: every admin page and API still performs its own permission check.

Figure 1. The Users page. The list is loaded from the users table; password fields are never rendered with the stored hash.

docs.title: 2. Accessing the Users Manager
docs.text:
The Users manager is available from the admin sidebar under Users.

Access to this page requires the users permission. Administrator accounts with the all permission can also access it. Users without the required permission will see a permission error message and will not be able to view the user list.

To open the page, click Users in the sidebar. The page displays a list of existing user accounts and provides several forms for account and password management.

docs.title: 3. Understanding the User List
docs.text:
The user list is loaded dynamically and shows the following information for each user:

  • Username – the login name of the user.
  • Permissions – the list of permissions assigned to that user.

Each row also includes Edit and Delete buttons if the current user has permission to manage users.

The list is displayed in a table format. If no users have been added, the page shows a “No data” message.

docs.title: 4. Adding a User
docs.text:
To add a new administrator account:

  1. Open the Users page.
  2. Click the Add User button.
  3. In the modal form, fill in the following fields:
Field Description Username The login name for the new user. This field is required. Password The initial password for the new account. Required for new users. Permissions Select one or more checkboxes to assign permissions.
  1. Click Save.

The new user is inserted into the users table with the password securely hashed. The user can now log in to the admin panel with the credentials you provided.

When creating a user, grant only the permissions that are necessary for that person’s role. For full administrative access, select the All permission. For limited roles, select only the relevant module permissions.

Figure 2. Add User. Select only the permissions required for the person's role.

docs.title: 5. Editing a User
docs.text:
To modify an existing user:

  1. Find the user in the user list.
  2. Click the Edit button in that row.
  3. The modal form opens with the current permissions filled in.
  4. Update the permissions as needed.
  5. Click Save.

The username field may be disabled when editing an existing user. The current implementation allows you to change permissions without resetting the password. If you need to change the username, you may need to create a new account or update the record directly in the database, depending on the current version.

Figure 3. Edit User. The username is normally fixed; permissions can be changed without resetting the password.

docs.title: 6. Deleting a User
docs.text:
To remove a user account:

  1. Find the user in the user list.
  2. Click the Delete button in that row.
  3. Confirm the deletion when prompted.

The user is permanently removed from the users table. This cannot be undone. Avoid deleting your own account while you are logged in, because you may lose access to the admin panel.

If you want to temporarily disable a user without deleting the account, consider changing the user’s permissions to an empty set or removing all module permissions. This effectively prevents the user from performing any administrative actions.

docs.title: 7. Password Management
docs.text: The Users page includes two password management forms. One is for changing your own password, and the other is for administrators to change another user’s password.

docs.title: 7.1 Changing Your Own Password
docs.text:
The Change My Password form allows the currently logged-in user to update their own password.

To change your password:

  1. Scroll to the Change My Password form on the Users page.
  2. Enter a new password in the New Password field.
  3. Repeat the password in the Confirm Password field.
  4. Click Update.

The system verifies that both password fields match before saving. After a successful change, the new password takes effect immediately.

If the account is still using the default password, the page displays a warning. This warning disappears once the password is changed.

docs.title: 7.2 Changing Another User’s Password
docs.text:
The Change Other User Password form is visible only to users with the all permission. This form allows an administrator to reset the password for any other account.

To change another user’s password:

  1. Select the target user from the Select User dropdown.
  2. Enter a new password.
  3. Repeat the password.
  4. Click Update.

This is useful when a user forgets their password or when you need to enforce a password reset.

Figure 4. Password management. The “Change Other User Password” form is only available with the all permission.

docs.title: 8. Permission Model
docs.text:
LabPress uses a flat permission model. Each user account has a list of strings that represent the modules they can access.

The following permission values are recognized by the core:

Permission Access Level all Full access to every admin page, setting, and action. publications Access to publications and news management. slides Access to slides management. tools Access to tool, project, and project category management. users Access to user management and password forms.

Users with the all permission automatically pass all permission checks, regardless of whether other permissions are also assigned. For example, assigning both all and tools is redundant.

Users without any permissions can still log in, but they will not see any management pages and will be denied access to all admin actions.

The permission checks are performed in the admin views and API endpoints using the hasPermission() function. If a user does not have the required permission, the system returns a permission error.

docs.title: 9. Security Recommendations
docs.text:
User accounts control access to the entire admin panel. Follow these recommendations to keep the site secure:

  • Change the default root password immediately after installation.
  • Use strong, unique passwords for all administrator accounts.
  • Grant the all permission only to trusted administrators.
  • Create limited accounts for staff members who only need to manage one module, such as publications or slides.
  • Regularly review the user list and remove accounts that are no longer needed.
  • Avoid sharing administrator credentials. Create separate accounts for each person who needs access.
  • If an account is compromised, change its password immediately and review the content for unauthorized changes.

The user management system uses PHP’s password_hash() and password_verify() functions with bcrypt hashing. Passwords are never stored in plain text.

docs.title: 10. Operational Checks
docs.text:
• At least one all account exists and its password is stored outside the repository.
  • The default root password has been changed.
  • A limited editor can log in but cannot open unrelated modules.
  • The public account dropdown hides modules the user cannot access.
  • Deleting an account does not remove the last administrator.
  • Password changes are verified with a fresh login, not only with an in-session form message.

If a user can see a menu item but receives a permission error after clicking it, check both the menu's declared permission and the view's own guard. The menu is not the authorization boundary.

docs.title: 11. Next Steps
docs.text:
After managing users, you may want to continue with:

  • Site Settings – configure site identity and homepage content.
  • Navigation Menus – manage header and footer menus.
  • Plugin Management – manage plugins and extensions.
  • Publications – manage academic publications.
  • Projects – manage research projects.
  • Research News – manage laboratory news.

docs.title: Configuration Layers
docs.text:
This chapter explains how LabPress stores and resolves configuration. It is aimed at administrators and developers who need to know which values belong in a file, which values belong in the database, and which layer wins when both exist.

For procedural setup, use Installation; for first-run checks, use Quick Start.

docs.title: 1. Two Configuration Layers
docs.text:
Layer Storage Examples Edited by Environment includes/config.php Database host/name/user/password, PHP session start, time zone Server operator, via file editor or deployment secret Site site_config table Site name, browser title format, default language, About Us, statistics, research cards Administrator, via Settings → Site Config Plugin state plugins table + plugin files Enabled/disabled status, plugin header metadata Administrator, via Plugins Runtime PHP INI / FPM pool Upload size, memory, execution time, error display Hosting panel or php.ini

Keep credentials in config.php, not in site_config. Keep editorial content in site_config, not in PHP files. This separation makes the database portable and keeps secrets out of admin exports.

flowchart LR
    A[Browser request] --> B[includes/config.php]
    B --> C[PDO + session]
    C --> D[includes/functions.php]
    D --> E[loadPlugins]
    E --> F[site_config + plugin state]
    F --> G[Page render]
    G --> H[Admin or frontend output]

docs.title: 2. Environment Configuration
docs.text:
includes/config.php is deployment-owned. It performs four jobs:

  1. starts the PHP session;
  2. defines the database constants;
  3. creates the shared PDO connection;
  4. sets the default time zone.
<?php
session_start();

define('DB_HOST', 'localhost');
define('DB_NAME', 'labpress');
define('DB_USER', 'labpress_user');
define('DB_PASS', 'replace-with-a-strong-password');

try {
    $pdo = new PDO(
        'mysql:host=' . DB_HOST . ';dbname=' . DB_NAME . ';charset=utf8mb4',
        DB_USER,
        DB_PASS,
        [
            PDO::ATTR_ERRMODE => PDO::ERRMODE_EXCEPTION,
            PDO::ATTR_DEFAULT_FETCH_MODE => PDO::FETCH_ASSOC,
            PDO::ATTR_EMULATE_PREPARES => false,
        ]
    );
} catch (PDOException $e) {
    die('Database Connect Error: ' . $e->getMessage());
}

date_default_timezone_set('Asia/Shanghai');

Rules:

  • DB_HOST is usually localhost; use a socket or remote host only when the database is not local.
  • DB_NAME must contain the imported LabPress schema.
  • DB_USER needs SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE on the LabPress database. DDL privileges are only needed for manual schema work.
  • Do not change the PDO options unless you understand the consequences. EMULATE_PREPARES => false keeps native prepared statements on.
  • config.php must not be committed with real credentials. It is intentionally deployment-specific.

docs.title: 3. PHP Runtime Settings
docs.text:
These values are not stored in site_config; they belong to the PHP process.

Directive Suggested value Why it matters upload_max_filesize 10M or higher Slide, project, and news images; plugin ZIPs. post_max_size Greater than upload_max_filesize The whole multipart request, not just the file. max_execution_time 60 or higher Larger imports and ZIP extraction. memory_limit 128M or higher Markdown rendering and larger result sets. display_errors Off in production Prevents path and SQL detail leakage. log_errors On Keeps diagnostics available without exposing them. file_uploads On Required for every upload endpoint. session.cookie_httponly 1 Reduces session theft via JavaScript. session.cookie_samesite Lax Basic CSRF hardening for browser flows.

The plugin installer page includes an environment panel. Use it to confirm zip, writable paths, and upload limits before debugging a failed installation.

docs.title: 4. Site Configuration Storage
docs.text:
Site settings live in site_config as key/value rows:

Column Meaning config_key Unique setting name. config_value Stored value. JSON is used for arrays such as statistics and research cards.

Core accessors:

LabPress::config($key, $default = '');
LabPress::setConfig($key, $value);

LabPress::config() loads the table once per request and caches it statically. A direct database edit therefore becomes visible on the next request, not in the current one.

docs.title: 5. Core Configuration Keys
docs.text:
These keys are normally edited through Settings → Site Config.

Key Type Used for site_name string Footer, admin sidebar, compact brand text. site_title string Full browser title and metadata. title_format string Pattern such as {page} - {site}. language locale Default site language and admin fallback. about_us HTML About Us section on the homepage. stat_items JSON array Homepage statistics: icon, label, value. research_title string Research direction section heading. research_subtitle string Research direction subheading. research_cards JSON array Research direction cards: icon, title, description. ml_source_locale locale Source locale used by Dynamic Multi-Language.

Plugins may add their own keys. Treat any ml_* key as plugin-owned and do not reuse it for unrelated content.

docs.title: 6. Plugin Configuration and Loading
docs.text:
Plugin state is split between files and the plugins table:

Column Meaning slug Directory name; must match plugins/{slug}/. name Display name parsed from the plugin header. description Short description parsed from the header. version Plugin version. author Plugin author. status 1 active, 0 inactive.

docs.title: 6.1 Load order
docs.text:
loadPlugins() reads active plugins once during bootstrap and includes each plugin.php. Plugin files register their hooks during inclusion. After all plugins are loaded, getLocale() runs; this ordering is required for admin_locale.

sequenceDiagram
    participant F as functions.php
    participant DB as plugins table
    participant P as plugin.php
    participant H as LabPress_Hooks
    participant L as getLocale

    F->>DB: SELECT active plugins
    F->>P: include each active plugin
    P->>H: addAction / addFilter
    F->>L: resolve locale after registration
    L->>H: applyFilters('admin_locale', ...)
    F->>H: doAction('init')

docs.title: 6.2 Plugin language files
docs.text:
Plugin language files are not merged into the core namespace. A plugin must request its own file:

__('ml_plugin_name', 'plugin:dynamic-multilang');

The plugin file lives at plugins/{slug}/languages/{locale}.php. A plugin that is deactivated simply has no callback; core strings continue to load from the root languages/ packs.

docs.title: 7. Internationalization Configuration
docs.text:
LabPress separates configuration for the two translation layers:

Question Where to look Which locale is active for this request? getLocale(); URL lang, cookie, or site default. Which locale does the admin use? admin_locale filter, implemented by Dynamic Multi-Language via ml_admin_locale. Where are framework strings? languages/{locale}/{module}.php. Where are plugin strings? plugins/{slug}/languages/{locale}.php, explicit plugin:{slug}. Where are database content translations? ml_translations, managed by Dynamic Multi-Language.

1.1.1 changed the core rule: plugin language files are not auto-merged. See Core Language Packs and Dynamic Multi-Language.

docs.title: 8. Frontend Resource Loading
docs.text:
Most resources are local:

  • assets/css/ and assets/js/ for the frontend;
  • admin/assets/ for the admin panel;
  • assets/fontawesome/ for icons;
  • admin/assets/js/easymde.min.js and admin/assets/css/easymde.min.css for Markdown editing;
  • assets/js/isotope.pkgd.min.js for project filtering.

There is no CDN dependency in the default theme. If a deployment blocks outbound requests, the site still loads its CSS, icons, and JavaScript from the local tree. If you add a CDN later, document the change in docs/getting-started/overview.md and verify both HTTP and HTTPS.

docs.title: Installation Guide
docs.text:
This guide walks through a first-time LabPress 1.1.1 installation on a typical PHP/MySQL host. It covers environment checks, source acquisition, database creation, sample-data import, includes/config.php, directory permissions, first login, and post-install verification.

If you are upgrading an existing 1.1.0 site rather than installing from scratch, use the 1.1.1 upgrade notes instead of re-importing the sample database.

docs.title: 1.1 Deployment model
docs.text:
LabPress is a flat-file PHP application. There is no installer wizard and no writable install/ directory. A deployment consists of:

  1. the project files in the web root (or a subdirectory);
  2. a MySQL database imported from labpressexample.sql;
  3. one deployment-owned includes/config.php;
  4. writable uploads/ and plugins/ directories.

The browser-facing entry points are /index.php and /admin/index.php. The default URL layout assumes the project is installed at the domain root. A subdirectory install works, but relative asset and upload paths should be checked after deployment.

flowchart TD
    A[Prepare PHP + MySQL] --> B[Download or clone LabPress]
    B --> C[Create empty database]
    C --> D[Import labpressexample.sql]
    D --> E[Edit includes/config.php]
    E --> F[Set uploads/plugins permissions]
    F --> G[Open the public homepage]
    G --> H[Log in to /admin]
    H --> I[Change the default password]
    I --> J[Configure site identity and menus]
    J --> K[Install or activate plugins]

docs.title: 1.2 Requirements
2. Obtaining the Source Code
docs.text: Choose one method. Both produce the same application tree; the ZIP is easier for a server without Git.

docs.title: 2.1 Clone the repository
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/GuiHui-huimy/LabPress.git
cd LabPress

Upload or move the project into the web root. If the web root is /www/wwwroot/LabPress, the repository root should be that directory, not a nested LabPress/LabPress directory.

docs.title: 2.2 Download the ZIP archive
docs.text: Download the latest release from GitHub Releases, extract it locally, and upload the extracted contents. Do not upload the outer folder if your panel already creates the site directory.

docs.title: 2.3 Verify the directory
docs.text:
A healthy source tree contains at least:

LabPress/
├── admin/                  # admin entry + views
├── api/                    # JSON endpoints
├── assets/                 # frontend CSS/JS/fonts
├── docs/                   # MkDocs source
├── includes/               # config, helpers, hooks, header/footer
├── languages/              # core language packs
├── plugins/                # plugin directories
├── uploads/                # runtime uploads
├── index.php
├── publications.php
├── tools.php
├── projects.php
├── news.php
├── labpressexample.sql
└── README.md

includes/config.php may be absent in a fresh clone because it is deployment-owned. Copy includes/config-sample.php to includes/config.php before editing if your package does not include one.

docs.title: 3. Database Setup and Sample Data
docs.text:
The SQL dump creates tables and inserts demo content. It does not create a database. Create an empty database first, then import.

The sample dump was exported from MySQL 8.0 and may contain utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci. MySQL 5.7 does not understand that collation; replace it with utf8mb4_general_ci before importing, or import into MySQL 8.0 and convert afterwards.

docs.title: 3.1 Method A: phpMyAdmin / BaoTa panel
docs.text:
This is the recommended path for shared hosting and panel-managed servers.

  1. Open the hosting panel and choose Database.
  2. Create a database, for example labpress.
  3. Set the character set to utf8mb4 and the collation to utf8mb4_general_ci.
  4. Create a database user with full privileges on that database, or reuse an existing user.
  5. Record the host, database name, username, and password.
  6. Open phpMyAdmin, select the new database, and choose Import.
  7. Choose labpressexample.sql, keep the format as SQL, and run the import.
  8. Confirm that tables such as publications, projects, news, tools, and users exist.

The database creation screen. Use utf8mb4 and a dedicated database user.

Give the user full privileges on the LabPress database only.

Select the empty database before importing the SQL dump.

The import form. Keep the SQL format and do not change the character set unless your panel requires it.

A successful import lists the LabPress tables and the demo records.

docs.title: 3.2 Method B: MySQL command line
docs.text:
Use this when you have shell access and prefer reproducible commands.

CREATE DATABASE labpress
    CHARACTER SET utf8mb4
    COLLATE utf8mb4_general_ci;

CREATE USER 'labpress_user'@'localhost'
    IDENTIFIED BY 'replace-with-a-strong-password';

GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON labpress.* TO 'labpress_user'@'localhost';
FLUSH PRIVILEGES;

Then import from the project root:

mysql -u labpress_user -p labpress < labpressexample.sql

Verify the result:

mysql -u labpress_user -p labpress -e "SHOW TABLES;"

If the command returns no error but the site is empty, confirm that the dump was imported into the same database named in DB_NAME.

docs.title: 4. Configure includes/config.php
docs.text: includes/config.php is the only file that should contain deployment-specific database credentials. It is intentionally excluded from version control in most deployments.

docs.title: 4.1 Create the file
docs.text:
From the project root:

cp includes/config-sample.php includes/config.php

If your package already contains config.php, back it up before editing:

cp includes/config.php includes/config.php.bak

docs.title: 4.2 Set the database constants
docs.text:
<?php
session_start();

// 1. Database host. Use "localhost" unless MySQL is on another host.
define('DB_HOST', 'localhost');

// 2. Database name created in the previous step.
define('DB_NAME', 'labpress');

// 3. Database user with privileges on that database.
define('DB_USER', 'labpress_user');

// 4. Database password.
define('DB_PASS', 'replace-with-a-strong-password');

try {
    $pdo = new PDO(
        'mysql:host=' . DB_HOST . ';dbname=' . DB_NAME . ';charset=utf8mb4',
        DB_USER,
        DB_PASS,
        [
            PDO::ATTR_ERRMODE => PDO::ERRMODE_EXCEPTION,
            PDO::ATTR_DEFAULT_FETCH_MODE => PDO::FETCH_ASSOC,
            PDO::ATTR_EMULATE_PREPARES => false,
        ]
    );
} catch (PDOException $e) {
    die('Database Connect Error: ' . $e->getMessage());
}

date_default_timezone_set('Asia/Shanghai');

The exact constant names and comments in config-sample.php are authoritative. Keep the PDO options unless you have a specific reason to change them.

docs.title: 4.3 Security rules for config.php
docs.text:
• Never commit real credentials. Add includes/config.php to .gitignore if it is not already ignored.
  • Do not include config.php in a public release ZIP.
  • Do not run git reset --hard or git checkout -- includes/config.php on a server where the file contains production credentials. Use skip-worktree or a deployment secret instead.
  • Restrict direct HTTP access to includes/ at the web-server level where possible.
  • Rotate the database password if the file was ever exposed.

docs.title: 5. Directory Permissions
docs.text:
The PHP process must be able to write uploaded images and plugin packages. Read access is required for the rest of the tree.

chmod -R 755 uploads/
chmod -R 755 plugins/

If the web server runs as a dedicated user, set ownership explicitly:

chown -R www-data:www-data uploads plugins

On a BaoTa-style panel, the site user may be www; use the actual PHP-FPM user. Avoid 777 on production. If uploads fail, check:

  1. the directory owner versus the PHP-FPM user;
  2. SELinux/AppArmor restrictions;
  3. the panel's “open_basedir” setting;
  4. PHP upload limits (upload_max_filesize, post_max_size).

docs.title: 6. First Access and Login
docs.text:
Open the public site:

https://your-domain/

You should see the demo homepage with slides, projects, publications, tools, and news. If the page is blank or reports Database Connect Error, fix includes/config.php before continuing.

The administration panel is at:

https://your-domain/admin/

The sample database creates one administrator:

Field Value Username root Password lab123456

The login page after installation. The 中文 / English control appears below the form when Dynamic Multi-Language is active.

The dashboard is the first screen after login. This v1.1.1 capture also shows the admin language switcher in the topbar. Change the default password before editing content.

Change the password immediately. Open Users → Change My Password, set a strong password, and confirm that isUsingDefaultPassword() no longer shows a warning. For a production site, create a separate administrator and stop using root for day-to-day work.

docs.title: 6.1 Post-install checklist
docs.text:
• The public homepage loads without PHP warnings.
  • /admin/login.php loads and accepts the sample login.
  • The default password has been changed.
  • uploads/ and plugins/ are writable by PHP.
  • includes/config.php is not web-accessible.
  • HTTPS is enabled and the admin cookie is sent over HTTPS.
  • The site name, title, and footer are correct under Settings → Site Config.
  • The navigation menu points to the intended pages.
  • Dynamic Multi-Language is active only if the site actually needs database-content translation.
  • A database backup has been taken after configuration.

docs.title: 7. Security Recommendations
docs.text:
• Use HTTPS for both frontend and admin. A valid certificate is not optional for a site with logins.
  • Change the sample root password before exposing the site to the internet.
  • Keep includes/config.php outside version control and outside public backups where possible.
  • Restrict includes/, docs/, and labpressexample.sql at the web-server level. None of them need to be publicly downloadable.
  • Back up the database and uploads/ together; restoring only the database leaves broken image references.
  • Keep PHP and MySQL patched. The application has no autoloader or third-party framework to update, but the runtime still needs maintenance.
  • Install plugins only from sources you trust. A plugin is PHP code with the same filesystem privileges as the site.

docs.title: The page is blank or reports a database error
docs.text: Check includes/config.php first. Confirm DB_HOST, DB_NAME, DB_USER, and DB_PASS; then confirm pdo_mysql is enabled. Temporarily enable PHP error display only in a local environment, never on a public production site.

docs.title: SQL import fails with a collation error
docs.text: Replace utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci with utf8mb4_general_ci in the dump, or import into MySQL 8.0. Do not mix collations across tables that join each other.

docs.title: Images do not load
docs.text: Confirm that uploads/ and images/ exist, contain the referenced files, and are readable by the web server. If the site is installed in a subdirectory, check that the database paths and the public URL prefix agree.

docs.title: Plugin ZIP installation fails
docs.text: Confirm that the zip PHP extension is enabled and that plugins/ is writable. The installer also checks the archive structure; a ZIP that contains an extra wrapper directory may need to be repacked with plugin.php at the archive root.

docs.title: The language switch does not change the admin panel
docs.text: Use /admin/login.php?lang=zh_CN as a direct test. If the HTML still reports lang="en-US", check the loadPlugins() / getLocale() order in includes/functions.php and clear OPcache. See Core Language Packs for the exact resolution order.

docs.title: git pull refuses because local files changed
docs.text: Do not discard includes/config.php. Inspect the changed files, stash only the disposable edits, pull, then restore the stash. On a server where config.php is skip-worktree, never use git reset --hard as a shortcut.

docs.title: LabPress Documentation Overview
docs.text:
Welcome to the LabPress documentation. This page is the technical and conceptual entry point for LabPress 1.1.1, an open-source academic content management system for research groups, university laboratories, and individual research teams.

The goal of this page is not to repeat installation steps. It explains what the system is, how a request moves through it, where the core/plugin/i18n boundaries sit, and which parts of the documentation you should read next. For hands-on setup, start with the Installation Guide; for a short first-run path, use Quick Start.

docs.title: 1. What LabPress Is
docs.text:
LabPress is a pure PHP + MySQL CMS with no framework, ORM, template engine, or Composer dependency. It ships with academic modules that a research site usually needs:

  • publications;
  • homepage slides;
  • software and database tools, including tool details and version history;
  • research projects with categories;
  • research news with Markdown content;
  • navigation menus and site settings;
  • users, permissions, and password management.

The frontend is rendered by standalone PHP entry files at the project root. The admin panel is a separate entry area under /admin/. Shared behavior lives in /includes/; plugins extend both surfaces through actions and filters.

The two features that most strongly distinguish LabPress from a generic CMS are:

  1. A hook-driven plugin system. Core output points are intentionally filterable, and plugins can register admin pages without editing core files.
  2. A deliberately split i18n model. Static interface strings come from core language packs; database content is handled by the Dynamic Multi-Language plugin. Admin and frontend locales are separate concerns.

docs.title: 2. Design Principles
docs.text: Principle Practical consequence Academic first Publications, projects, tools, versions, and research news are first-class data models, not generic “posts”. Core stays plugin-agnostic Removing every plugin still leaves a working site. Core only exposes hooks and safe fallbacks. Explicit boundaries Plugin language files do not merge into the core namespace. Plugin strings use plugin:{slug}. Separate frontend and admin contexts The public site and the admin panel have independent entry points, assets, permissions, and locale policies. Low operational cost A standard PHP/MySQL host is enough. There is no build step, queue, daemon, or external service requirement. Content is editable without SQL Site settings, navigation, slides, and academic modules all have admin views.

docs.title: 3. Technology Stack
docs.text: Layer Technology Notes Runtime PHP 7.4+ No framework; PDO for database access. Database MySQL 5.7+ / MariaDB 10.3+ UTF-8 (utf8mb4) tables. Frontend HTML5, CSS3, vanilla JavaScript EasyMDE and Isotope are bundled; Font Awesome is served from the local assets/fontawesome/ directory. Admin UI PHP views + CSS + vanilla JavaScript Modal forms and table views; no React/Vue build. Plugin API LabPress_Hooks WordPress-style actions and filters. Markdown Parsedown (bundled) Used for news and project bodies. Authentication PHP sessions + bcrypt password_hash() / password_verify(); permission checks in admin views and APIs. i18n Core language packs + ml_translations Static UI strings and database content are separate layers.

docs.title: 4. Architecture at a Glance
docs.text:
The important detail in 1.1.1 is boot order: plugins are loaded before the early locale resolution. That is what allows a plugin to answer the admin_locale filter on the very first request.

flowchart LR
    B[Browser] --> F[Frontend entry<br/>index.php, news.php, ...]
    B --> A[Admin entry<br/>admin/index.php or login.php]
    F --> C[includes/config.php<br/>session + PDO]
    A --> C
    C --> FN[includes/functions.php<br/>helpers + hooks + i18n]
    FN --> PL[loadPlugins]
    PL --> DB[(MySQL<br/>plugins table)]
    PL --> P[Plugin files<br/>register actions/filters]
    P --> LOC[getLocale<br/>admin_locale filter]
    LOC --> INIT[init action]
    INIT --> R[Render page]
    R --> DB
    R --> H[applyFilters / doAction]
    H --> OUT[HTML response]

A request is therefore not a single “core render”. It is a small pipeline:

  1. Bootstrap. The entry file requires config.php (session and PDO) and functions.php (helpers, hook registry, i18n).
  2. Plugin discovery. loadPlugins() reads the enabled plugin list and includes each plugin.php.
  3. Registration. Plugin files register filters and actions while they are included.
  4. Locale resolution. getLocale() runs after plugin registration. In the admin context it applies admin_locale; in the frontend context it reads lang, then cookie, then site default.
  5. Init. LabPress_Hooks::doAction('init') runs after locale setup.
  6. Render. The page queries the database, applies filters at output points, and returns HTML.

A more concrete frontend request looks like this:

sequenceDiagram
    participant U as Browser
    participant E as index.php
    participant C as config.php
    participant F as functions.php
    participant P as Enabled plugins
    participant D as MySQL

    U->>E: GET /?lang=zh_CN
    E->>C: start session, connect PDO
    E->>F: load helpers and hook registry
    F->>D: read enabled plugin list
    F->>P: include plugin.php files
    P->>F: addAction / addFilter
    F->>F: getLocale() after plugins
    F->>P: doAction('init')
    E->>D: query page content
    E->>P: applyFilters('translate', ...)
    E->>P: applyFilters('slides_data', ...)
    E->>U: HTML + header/footer hooks

docs.title: 5.1 Core owns framework strings
docs.text: The core language packs under languages/{locale}/ contain only labels, buttons, validation messages, and default template text. In 1.1.1, __() no longer scans every active plugin and merges its language array into the core namespace.

docs.title: 5.2 Plugins own plugin strings
docs.text:
A plugin language file lives at:

plugins/{plugin-slug}/languages/{locale}.php

It is loaded only when the caller names the plugin explicitly:

__('ml_plugin_name', 'plugin:dynamic-multilang');

A plugin should also use a unique key prefix. Explicit loading prevents path collisions; the prefix prevents semantic collisions inside the plugin's own namespace.

docs.title: 5.3 Dynamic content is a separate layer
docs.text:
Database content (navigation titles, slide text, About Us, research directions, statistics labels) is translated by the Dynamic Multi-Language plugin. It is not stored in PHP language files and it is not merged into the core namespace.

flowchart TB
    subgraph Static["Static UI layer"]
        K[Core __ function] --> LF["languages/{locale}/{module}.php"]
        K --> PF["plugins/{slug}/languages/{locale}.php"]
    end
    subgraph Dynamic["Dynamic content layer"]
        T[translate filter] --> ML[ml_translations]
        T --> ORIG[Original database value]
    end
    UI[Page output] --> K
    UI --> T
    K --> UI
    T --> UI

The practical rule for developers is simple: if the string is written in PHP/HTML by the framework, use a core or plugin language pack. If the string is typed by an administrator into the database, use the Dynamic Multi-Language plugin.

docs.title: 5.4 Admin locale is plugin-owned
docs.text:
The core provides the admin_locale filter and a safe fallback to the site default. The Dynamic Multi-Language plugin implements the filter and stores the selection in ml_admin_locale. If the plugin is absent, the admin panel still works and simply follows the site default.

See Internationalization Overview and Core Language Packs for the full contracts.

docs.title: 6. Directory Map
docs.text:
The following map focuses on the files that matter when reading or extending the system. Generated uploads and documentation theme internals are omitted.

LabPress/
├── admin/
│   ├── index.php                 # Admin entry, menu + view loader
│   ├── login.php                 # Login, redirect handling, locale switch hook
│   ├── logout.php

│   │   └── admin-footer.php

│   └── assets/                   # admin CSS/JS, EasyMDE
├── api/
│   ├── data.php                  # read endpoint
│   ├── save.php                  # write endpoint
│   ├── upload.php                # image upload

The exact set of frontend entry files may grow as modules are added. The rule is stable: each public page is a standalone PHP entry file that includes shared config/helpers and calls the hook system at its output points.

docs.title: 7. Documentation Map
docs.text:
The MkDocs navigation mirrors the operational lifecycle of the project:

Section Read it when you need to… Getting Started install, configure, or upgrade the system Setup configure site identity, menus, plugins, and styling Content Management manage publications, slides, tools, projects, news, and users Internationalization understand the two translation layers and admin/frontend locale split Plugin Development build, register, and ship a plugin Reference inspect endpoints, tables, and developer helpers Security review deployment hardening and reporting boundaries Changelog check version changes and upgrade notes

The pages are intentionally cross-linked. A content page explains the admin workflow and then points to the relevant API/i18n reference; an i18n page explains the contract and then points to the exact plugin file. Use the table above as a map, not as a reading order.

docs.title: 9. What Changed in 1.1.1 That Affects Readers
docs.text:
• The admin language switch is now genuinely independent from the public lang cookie. Do not test it only by switching the frontend; test /admin/login.php?lang=zh_CN and reload the panel.
  • Plugin language files must be requested with plugin:{slug}. If you are porting an older plugin that relied on automatic merging, move its strings into its own languages/{locale}.php and update every __() call.
  • The public navigation account entry is rendered by includes/header.php. It is visible on every public page, not only the homepage.
  • admin/login.php accepts redirect=home. The value is allow-listed; arbitrary URLs are ignored.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
This guide is for a LabPress that is already installed, whose database has been imported, and whose includes/config.php connects successfully. It covers the minimum sequence needed to turn the sample site into a usable deployment.

Detailed module behavior lives in the chapter pages; this page focuses on order, verification, and the first-run decisions that are easy to postpone.

flowchart TD
    A[Log in at /admin] --> B[Change the default password]
    B --> C[Review site identity and homepage settings]
    C --> D[Review navigation labels and URLs]
    D --> E[Activate only the plugins you need]
    E --> F[Verify admin and frontend locales]
    F --> G[Edit or create one item per module]
    G --> H[Verify the public pages and account entry]
    H --> I[Take a backup]

docs.title: 1. Log In to the Admin Panel
docs.text:
Open:

https://your-domain/admin/

Use the sample administrator:

Field Value Username root Password lab123456

After login, the dashboard shows the current content counts. A fresh sample database is not an empty site; it contains demo publications, slides, tools, projects, news, and users.

The dashboard after the first login. Content counts are read from the live database; the topbar shows the v1.1.1 admin language switcher and account chip.

The login page in v1.1.1. The 中文 / English control below the form belongs to Dynamic Multi-Language; it changes the admin interface, not the public site.

docs.title: 2. Secure the Default Administrator
docs.text:
The sample password is public. Change it before doing anything else:

  1. Open Users in the admin sidebar.
  2. Use Change My Password.
  3. Enter a strong password and confirm it.
  4. Reload the page and confirm the default-password warning is gone.

For a production site, create a separate administrator account and stop using root for daily editing. The root account can remain as a break-glass account, but its password must be unique.

User management contains the self-service password form and the administrator password reset form.

See Users Management for the permission model.

docs.title: 3. Review Site Settings
docs.text:
Open Settings → Site Config. Check:

  • site name and browser title;
  • default site language;
  • About Us copy;
  • statistics labels and values;
  • research direction cards;
  • footer text if FooterInfo is active.

The sample values are placeholders. Replace them before inviting visitors, because the homepage and every page title inherit these settings.

Site settings control the public identity of the site and several homepage sections.

See Site Settings for field-by-field guidance.

docs.title: 4. Review Navigation Before Content
docs.text:
Open Settings → Navigation Menus. Confirm that each menu item points to the intended page or external URL.

A typical first-run menu:

Label URL Target Home /index.php Same window Publications /publications.php Same window Tools /tools.php Same window Projects /projects.php Same window News /news.php Same window Contact External lab or university page New window

The navigation is stored in the database and rendered by includes/header.php. The header also renders the language switcher and the account entry; those are not separate menu records.

See Navigation Menus for CRUD and account-entry behavior.

docs.title: 5. Activate Only the Plugins You Need
docs.text:
Open Plugins → Installed Plugins.

LabPress ships with:

  • FooterInfo — footer text and simple footer styling.
  • Dynamic Multi-Language — database-content translation and the backend language switcher.
  • hello-word — a development example, safe to leave inactive.

Activate FooterInfo if you need editable footer content. Activate Dynamic Multi-Language only if the site actually serves more than one content language; otherwise it adds an admin page and translation tables that are not being used.

If a plugin directory exists but is not listed, use Scan for new plugins first. If activation fails, check the plugin header and the plugins table before uploading a new copy.

docs.title: 6. Verify Both Language Contexts
docs.text: LabPress 1.1.1 separates the frontend language from the admin language. Test both, not just the public switcher.

docs.title: Frontend
docs.text:
1. Open the homepage.
  2. Switch the language in the header.
  3. Reload. The selected locale should persist in the lang cookie.
  4. Check that database content (slide text, nav labels) changes only when Dynamic Multi-Language is active and translations exist.

docs.title: Admin
docs.text:
1. Open /admin/login.php?lang=zh_CN.
  2. Confirm the login page renders Chinese text and <html lang="zh-CN">.
  3. Log in and confirm the admin topbar remains Chinese.
  4. Switch back to English from the admin topbar or login-page switcher.
  5. Reload the page. The admin locale should persist independently of the frontend cookie.

If the admin language does not change, see the locale-order troubleshooting in Core Language Packs.

The Dynamic Multi-Language page is where database-content translations are edited.

For the architecture, see Internationalization Overview.

docs.title: 7. Create or Edit One Item per Module
docs.text:
Do not start by bulk-importing production content. Exercise one item in each module first; this exposes field mapping, image upload, and permission issues while the sample data is still available.

Suggested order:

  1. Slides — replace one homepage slide and confirm the carousel updates.
  2. Publications — add one paper and check the public list.
  3. Projects — create one category and one project; confirm filtering.
  4. Tools — add one tool, its detail record, and one version.
  5. News — publish one Markdown item with an image.
  6. Users — create a non-admin editor with a limited permission set.

The module pages contain field tables and validation notes:

  • Publications
  • Slides
  • Tools
  • Projects
  • Research News
  • Users

docs.title: 8. Verify the Public Account Entry
docs.text:
The public navigation is shared by all frontend pages. In 1.1.1 it contains an account entry in includes/header.php.

  1. Sign out of the admin panel.
  2. Open the homepage. The nav bar should show Sign in, not a username.
  3. Click Sign in. The link should include redirect=home.
  4. Log in. The browser should return to /index.php, not /admin/index.php.
  5. The nav bar should now show the username.
  6. Hover over the username. The dropdown should show Dashboard and only the admin modules permitted for that account.
  7. Click the username. It should open /admin/index.php.

If the username does not appear, check $_SESSION['user'] and the cookie path. If the dropdown is empty, check the permissions array stored for the user.

docs.title: 9. Take a Baseline Backup
docs.text:
After the site identity, navigation, and one sample item per module are correct, export the database and archive uploads/. Store them outside the web root.

This baseline is useful for two reasons:

  • it captures a known-good configuration before bulk content entry;
  • it gives you a rollback point before plugin experiments or a future upgrade.

docs.title: 10. Next Steps
docs.text:
• Configure every field: Site Settings.
  • Tune the menu and account entry: Navigation Menus.
  • Understand plugin safety: Plugin Management.
  • Read the release changes: Changelog 1.1.1.
  • Harden the deployment: Security.

docs.title: Core Language Packs
docs.text:
This chapter provides a technical reference for the core language pack system in LabPress. It describes how language files are structured, how the translation function works, how modules are loaded, and how the core interacts with the hook system to support both static and dynamic translation workflows.

The information in this chapter is intended for developers and advanced administrators who need to understand, extend, or modify the built-in internationalization behavior. It assumes familiarity with the general i18n architecture described in the Internationalization Overview.

docs.title: 1. Overview
docs.text:
LabPress uses a file-based language pack system for all static interface strings. Each supported locale has a dedicated directory under languages/, and each functional module has its own PHP file within that directory.

The system is built around a single translation function, __(), which:

  • Loads language files on demand.
  • Resolves translation keys, including nested keys using dot notation.
  • Applies the translate filter to the resolved value.
  • Falls back to the original key when no translation is found.

Language packs are loaded separately from the database-backed translation system provided by the Dynamic Multi-Language plugin. Together, they cover both static and dynamic content.

flowchart LR
    A[__ key, module] --> B{module starts with plugin:?}
    B -->|No| C[languages/locale/common.php]
    C --> D[languages/locale/module.php]
    D --> E[dot-path lookup]
    B -->|Yes| F[plugins/slug/languages/locale.php]
    F --> G[lookup inside plugin array]
    E --> H[translate filter]
    G --> H
    H --> I[return string or key]

The diagram shows the important v1.1.1 boundary: a plugin file is never merged into the core array. It is read only for the current call and only when the caller asks for plugin:{slug}.

docs.title: 2. Directory Structure
docs.text:
The core language files are organized as follows:

languages/
├── zh_CN/
│   ├── lang.config
│   ├── common.php
│   ├── index.php
│   ├── admin.php
│   ├── news.php
│   ├── projects.php
│   ├── tools.php
│   └── publications.php
└── en_US/
    ├── lang.config
    ├── common.php
    ├── index.php
    ├── admin.php
    ├── news.php
    ├── projects.php
    ├── tools.php
    └── publications.php

Each language directory contains:

  • A lang.config file that provides metadata about the language.
  • One or more module files named after the corresponding functional area.

Modules are organized by context. For example:

Module Purpose common Shared strings used across the site, including navigation, footer, buttons, and general labels index Strings specific to the homepage template admin Strings used in the administration panel, including menus, forms, and messages news Strings used by the research news module projects Strings used by the project and category pages tools Strings used by the tools module publications Strings used by the publications module

Plugins may define their own language directories and are not required to follow the core module names.

docs.title: 3. Language Metadata
docs.text:
Each language directory contains a lang.config file. This file returns a PHP array with metadata that is used when rendering the frontend language switcher and, when the Dynamic Multi-Language plugin is active, the admin language switcher.

A typical lang.config file looks like this:

<?php
return [
    'name'      => 'English',
    'locale'    => 'en_US',
    'flag'      => '🇺🇸',
    'direction' => 'ltr',
];

The locale value should match the directory name exactly. The getAvailableLanguages() function reads this file and appends the locale key from the directory name, ensuring consistency.

The metadata is used by:

  • The frontend language switcher.
  • The Site Language dropdown in the admin settings page.
  • The Dynamic Multi-Language plugin’s source locale selector.

docs.title: 4. Language File Format
docs.text:
Each language file must return an associative array. The keys are translation identifiers, and the values are the translated strings.

A simple language file looks like this:

<?php
return [
    'learn_more'      => 'Learn More',
    'view_details'    => 'View Details',
    'loading'         => 'Loading...',
    'footer_copyright'=> '© 2017-{year} HUI-MY.LAB. All rights reserved.',
];

The values may contain placeholders such as {year} or {site}. These placeholders are replaced by the relevant rendering code at output time, not by the translation function itself.

docs.title: 4.1 Nested Keys
docs.text:
Language files may use nested arrays to group related strings. The __() function supports accessing nested values using dot notation.

For example, a language file may define:

return [
    'nav' => [
        'home'         => 'Home',
        'tools'        => 'Tools',
        'publications' => 'Publications',
    ],
    'footer' => [
        'links' => [
            'blog'   => 'Blog',
            'forum'  => 'Forum',
        ],
    ],
];

To retrieve Home, the key would be:

__('nav.home', 'common');

The dot notation is resolved by splitting the key on . and traversing the array structure.

docs.title: 5. The Translation Function
docs.text:
The core translation function is defined in includes/functions.php:

function __($key, $module = 'common')

It accepts two parameters:

  • $key – the translation key. Supports dot notation for nested arrays.
  • $module – the module name. Defaults to common.

The function maintains static caches for:

  • Loaded core modules.
  • Merged core language data.

This design ensures that language files are loaded only once per PHP request.

docs.title: 6. Module Loading
docs.text: The translation function loads language files in a specific order.

docs.title: 6.1 Common Module
docs.text: The common module is loaded first and always. On the first call to __(), the system loads the common language file for the current locale and merges it into the local language array.

docs.title: 6.2 Explicit Core Module
docs.text:
If the $module argument is a core module name other than common, the corresponding file is loaded on demand.

For example:

__('page_title', 'publications');

This call loads languages/{locale}/publications.php and merges its contents into the current request’s language data.

docs.title: 6.3 Plugin Language Modules
docs.text:
Plugin language files are never merged into the core language namespace automatically. The core __() function only loads files under languages/{locale}/, plus the explicitly requested plugin file when the module starts with plugin:.

__('ml_plugin_name', 'plugin:dynamic-multilang');

When the module begins with plugin:, the translation function:

  1. Extracts the plugin directory name from the module string.
  2. Builds the path to the plugin's language file.
  3. Loads only that file.
  4. Resolves the key within that file's returned array.
  5. Returns the result directly without merging the plugin language data into the global core language array.

This explicit loading method isolates plugin translations and prevents a plugin language file from overwriting core keys. A plugin that is deactivated or whose directory is removed simply has no language callback; core strings keep coming from the root language packs.

Locale resolution order matters for backend language filters. getLocale() caches its result for the request, so any early call must happen after loadPlugins(). The core entry file resolves a requested lang after plugins are loaded; otherwise admin_locale callbacks would not be registered yet and the site default locale would be cached first.

docs.title: 7. Key Resolution and Fallback
docs.text:
After the necessary language data has been loaded, the translation function resolves the requested key.

If the key contains dot notation, it is split into segments. Each segment is used to traverse the language array. If a segment is missing, the function returns the original key and applies the translate filter.

If the key exists, the resolved value is passed through the translate filter before being returned.

The fallback behavior is important. If a language file is missing or incomplete, the site does not crash. Instead, untranslated strings appear in their original key form. This makes it easy to identify missing translations during development.

docs.title: 8. The translate Filter
docs.text:
Every value returned by __() is passed through the translate filter.

return LabPress_Hooks::applyFilters('translate', $value, $key, $locale, $module);

The filter receives four arguments:

  • $value – the resolved translation or the original key if no translation was found.
  • $key – the original translation key.
  • $locale – the current locale.
  • $module – the requested module.

Plugins can register on this filter to modify translations dynamically. The Dynamic Multi-Language plugin uses this filter to replace database-stored content with translated values.

docs.title: 9. Locale Detection
docs.text:
The current locale is determined by the getLocale() function. The function uses a static cache to avoid repeated detection within a single request.

The detection logic depends on the request context.

docs.title: 9.1 Admin Context
docs.text: In the admin area, getLocale() applies the admin_locale filter to the site default language. If no plugin handles the filter, or if the returned locale is not in the available list, it returns the site default. This is determined by checking the IS_ADMIN constant or the script path.

docs.title: 9.2 Frontend Context
docs.text:
In the frontend, the locale is selected in the following priority order:

  1. The lang URL parameter.
  2. The lang cookie.
  3. The site default language stored in site_config.

If the lang parameter is present and valid, the selected locale is stored in a cookie for future visits.

docs.title: 10. Language Discovery
docs.text:
The getAvailableLanguages() function scans the languages/ directory and reads each subdirectory’s lang.config file.

The returned array contains one entry per language, with the locale key set to the directory name.

This function is used by:

  • The frontend language switcher.
  • The admin language settings page.
  • The Dynamic Multi-Language plugin.

Adding a new language is therefore as simple as creating a new directory with a valid lang.config file and the necessary language files.

docs.title: 11. Adding a New Language
docs.text:
To add a new core language:

  1. Create a new directory under languages/. Use the locale code as the directory name, for example fr_FR.
  2. Create a lang.config file with the language metadata.
  3. Create a common.php file with the shared interface strings.
  4. Create additional module files as needed: index.php, admin.php, news.php, projects.php, tools.php, and publications.php.
  5. If the language should be available in the admin panel, ensure that the admin.php file covers all admin interface keys.

The new language will be detected automatically by getAvailableLanguages() and will appear in the frontend language switcher. It also appears in the admin switcher while the Dynamic Multi-Language plugin is active, because the plugin renders that control and handles admin_locale; without the plugin the backend stays on the site default language.

docs.title: 12. Integration with the Hook System
docs.text:
The core language system exposes several hooks that allow plugins to interact with translation data.

Hook Type Description translate Filter Applied to every string returned by __(). Can be used to replace strings with translations from other sources. admin_locale Filter Applied to the backend default locale. Receives the default locale and the list of available locale codes. Returning an invalid locale falls back to the site default, so core works without a locale plugin. page_title_full Filter Applied to the generated full page title. Can be used to customize title output.

Plugin developers should use these hooks instead of modifying core language files. This preserves compatibility and ensures that custom translation logic remains independent of the core.

docs.title: 13. Related Functions
docs.text:
The following functions are part of the core language system and are defined in includes/functions.php:

Function Description __($key, $module = 'common') Returns a translated string. _e($key, $module = 'common') Echoes a translated string. getLocale() Returns the current locale. getAvailableLanguages() Returns metadata for all available languages. getFullTitle($pageTitle = '', $suffix = '') Generates a complete page title using the configured format.

These functions form the foundation of the static translation system and are used throughout the core templates and admin panel.

docs.title: 14. Operational Checks
docs.text:
• Every core module file returns an array and contains no output before return.
  • Keys use dot notation only for actual nested arrays, not as literal key names.
  • A plugin string uses plugin:{slug} and resolves after activation.
  • Deactivating the plugin does not remove core translations.
  • getLocale() is first called after loadPlugins() on admin requests.
  • admin_locale rejects unknown locales instead of caching them.
  • The <html lang> attribute matches the resolved locale.
  • Missing keys are visible in development, not silently blank.

If a translated page shows a key instead of text, test the exact __() call in isolation. Check the module name first, the locale directory second, and the key path third. Editing the language file will not help if the caller is loading the wrong module.

docs.title: 15. Next Steps
docs.text:
After understanding the core language pack system, continue with:

  • Dynamic Multi-Language Plugin – learn how database-stored content is translated.
  • Plugin Development – understand how plugins can provide their own language files.
  • Hooks Reference – see the complete list of available hooks.
  • Plugin Examples – view working examples of plugins that use the translation system.

docs.title: Dynamic Multi-Language Plugin
docs.text:
This chapter provides a technical reference for the Dynamic Multi-Language plugin included with LabPress. The plugin extends the core internationalization system by enabling translation of database-stored content, such as navigation menus, slides, site configuration fields, and plugin-specific interface strings.

The chapter is intended for developers and advanced administrators who need to understand how the plugin works, how it stores translations, and how it interacts with the LabPress hook system. It assumes familiarity with the Internationalization Overview and Core Language Packs.

docs.title: 1. Overview
docs.text:
The Dynamic Multi-Language plugin solves a limitation of the core language pack system: core language files can only translate static strings that exist in the codebase. They cannot translate content created through the admin panel, such as navigation menu titles, homepage slide text, or the About Us field.

The plugin provides a translation management interface for this database-stored content. It does not modify the original records; instead, it stores translations in a separate table and replaces the output at render time using filters.

The plugin is packaged as a standard LabPress plugin located in:

plugins/dynamic-multilang/

Its slug, used in the plugins table and the plugin language loading mechanism, is dynamic-multilang.

docs.title: 2. Plugin Structure
docs.text:
The plugin directory contains the following files:

dynamic-multilang/
├── plugin.php
├── admin-page.php
├── languages/
│   ├── zh_CN.php
│   └── en_US.php
└── assets/
    └── dm-admin.css
  • plugin.php – main plugin file containing hooks, filters, and utility functions.
  • admin-page.php – callback for the admin management page.
  • languages/ – plugin language files for interface strings.
  • assets/ – admin styles and scripts.

The plugin header in plugin.php declares the plugin name, description, version, and author. This metadata is read by the plugin scanner when the plugin is first registered.

docs.title: 3. Translation Storage
docs.text:
All translations are stored in the ml_translations table. The table is created during plugin activation and dropped during uninstallation.

The table structure is:

Column Type Description id int Primary key, auto-increment table_name varchar(50) Logical source of the original string, such as nav_menu, slides, site_config, __custom, or plugin_dynamic-multilang record_id varchar(100) Unique identifier of the original record, or the original string itself for custom keys field_name varchar(100) Field within the record, such as title, description, config_value, or text locale varchar(10) Target language code, such as en_US translated_value text The translated text

A unique constraint is defined on the combination of table_name, record_id, field_name, and locale, preventing duplicate translations for the same source field and language.

erDiagram
    ml_translations {
        int id PK
        varchar table_name
        varchar record_id
        varchar field_name
        varchar locale
        text translated_value
    }

The table is a sidecar, not a replacement. nav_menu, slides, and site_config keep their source values; ml_translations holds only target-language overrides. Deleting a translation row therefore restores the source value without any data migration.

docs.title: 4. Core Functions
docs.text: The plugin defines several utility functions in plugin.php.

docs.title: 4.1 Source Locale Management
docs.text:
function ml_get_source_locale()

Returns the current source locale. The source locale represents the language in which the original site content is written. It first checks the ml_source_locale key in site_config. If that key is not set, it falls back to the site default language.

function ml_set_source_locale($locale)

Stores the source locale value in site_config using LabPress::setConfig().

docs.title: 4.2 Retrieving Translations
docs.text:
function ml_get_translation($table, $recordId, $field, $locale = null)

Retrieves a translation from the ml_translations table. If $locale is not provided, the current frontend locale is used.

The function first checks whether the requested locale is the same as the source locale. If it is, the function returns null, indicating that no translation should be applied and the original content should be used.

If the locale is different, the function queries the table for a matching translation. If no row is found, it returns null.

docs.title: 4.3 Saving Translations
docs.text:
function ml_set_translation($table, $recordId, $field, $locale, $value)

Saves a translation. If the value is empty, the corresponding row is deleted from the table. Otherwise, the function performs an upsert using INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE, updating the existing translation if one is present.

docs.title: 5. Filters and Integration
docs.text: The plugin registers its filters during the init action. This ensures that the plugin’s callbacks are only added after all plugins have been loaded.

docs.title: 5.1 Navigation Menu Translation
docs.text:
The plugin registers a filter on nav_menu_item:

LabPress_Hooks::addFilter('nav_menu_item', function($html, $menu) {
    $id = $menu['id'] ?? null;
    if (!$id) return $html;
    $newTitle = ml_get_translation('nav_menu', $id, 'title');
    if ($newTitle === null) return $html;
    return sprintf('<a href="%s">%s</a>', htmlspecialchars($menu['url']), htmlspecialchars($newTitle));
}, 10, 2);

The filter receives the generated HTML for a menu item and the raw menu data array. It checks whether a translation exists for the menu ID in the nav_menu table. If found, it regenerates the anchor tag with the translated title.

docs.title: 5.2 Slide Translation
docs.text:
The plugin registers a filter on slides_data:

LabPress_Hooks::addFilter('slides_data', function($slides) {
    foreach ($slides as &$slide) {
        $id = $slide['id'] ?? null;
        if ($id) {
            $title = ml_get_translation('slides', $id, 'title');
            $desc = ml_get_translation('slides', $id, 'description');
            if ($title) $slide['title'] = $title;
            if ($desc) $slide['description'] = $desc;
        }
    }
    return $slides;
});

This filter is applied when the frontend loads slide data from the API. It iterates over each slide and replaces the title and description if translations exist.

docs.title: 5.3 Dynamic Text Translation
docs.text: The plugin registers two filters on translate to handle dynamic content.

docs.title: Custom Keys and Site Configuration
docs.text:
LabPress_Hooks::addFilter('translate', function($value, $key) {
    if (defined('IS_ADMIN') || strpos($_SERVER['SCRIPT_NAME'], '/admin/') !== false) {
        return $value;
    }

    $trans = ml_get_translation('__custom', $key, 'text');
    if ($trans) return $trans;

    $siteMap = [
        'about_us'          => 'about_us',
        'about_us_content'  => 'about_us',
        'research_title'    => 'research_title',
        'research_heading'  => 'research_title',
        'research_subtitle' => 'research_subtitle',
        'research_subheading'=> 'research_subtitle',
    ];

    if (isset($siteMap[$key])) {
        $trans = ml_get_translation('site_config', $siteMap[$key], 'config_value');
        if ($trans) return $trans;
    }

    return $value;
}, 10, 2);

This filter is the core mechanism for translating user-edited content.

It first checks whether the current request is for the admin panel. If so, it returns the original value immediately, ensuring that administrators always see the source content when editing.

Then it looks for a custom translation in the __custom table. The record_id is the original string itself. This is used for dynamic text such as statistics labels and research card titles.

If no custom translation exists, the filter applies a mapping of core translation keys to site_config fields. For example, the key about_us maps to the about_us site configuration field. If a translation exists for that field, it is returned.

docs.title: Plugin Interface Translation
docs.text:
A second translate filter handles the plugin’s own interface strings:

LabPress_Hooks::addFilter('translate', function($value, $key, $locale) {
    $trans = ml_get_translation('plugin_dynamic-multilang', $key, 'plugin_text', $locale);
    if ($trans !== null) return $trans;
    return $value;
}, 10, 3);

This filter checks the plugin_dynamic-multilang table for translations of plugin-specific keys. It allows the admin interface of the plugin itself to be translated through the same management page.

docs.title: 5.4 Admin Locale and Switchers
docs.text:
The plugin owns the optional backend language policy. It registers a filter on admin_locale during plugin load, before any core admin translation is requested:

LabPress_Hooks::addFilter('admin_locale', 'ml_admin_locale', 10, 2);

ml_admin_locale() resolves the backend locale in this order:

  1. A valid lang query parameter on an admin request.
  2. The ml_admin_locale value stored in the current session.
  3. The ml_admin_locale cookie.
  4. The site default locale passed in by the core getLocale() function.

A valid selection is written to the session and to a dedicated ml_admin_locale cookie. The cookie is separate from the frontend lang cookie, so changing the admin language does not change the public site language.

flowchart TD
    A[Admin request] --> B{lang query valid?}
    B -->|Yes| C[Use requested locale]
    B -->|No| D{Session value valid?}
    D -->|Yes| E[Use session locale]
    D -->|No| F{Cookie valid?}
    F -->|Yes| G[Use cookie locale]
    F -->|No| H[Site default locale]
    C --> I[Write session + cookie]
    I --> E
    E --> J[Set html lang + interface strings]
    G --> J
    H --> J

The query parameter is the immediate override used by the login-page switcher. The session keeps the choice across admin navigation; the cookie keeps it across browser restarts until it expires. If all three sources are absent, the site default is used, which is also the behavior when the plugin is inactive.

The plugin renders its switcher through two core hooks:

  • admin_topbar_actions in admin/index.php, after the user chip.
  • login_after_form in admin/login.php, below the login and back-home buttons.

If the plugin is inactive or removed, no admin_locale callback exists. The core getLocale() function then falls back to the site default locale, so the login page and admin console continue to work without any plugin dependency.

docs.title: 6. Admin Management Page
docs.text:
The plugin registers an admin page using LabPress::registerAdminPage():

LabPress::registerAdminPage('dynamic-multilang', __('ml_plugin_name', 'plugin:dynamic-multilang'), function() {
    require_once __DIR__ . '/admin-page.php';
});

The page is accessible from the admin sidebar and requires the all permission. The page title, like the rest of the plugin's interface, is loaded through the explicit plugin:dynamic-multilang language module.

The admin page organizes translations into several tabs:

  • Nav Menus – translations for header and footer menu titles.
  • Slides – translations for slide titles and descriptions.
  • About / Research – translations for About Us, research title, and research subtitle.
  • Dynamic Content – translations for statistics labels and research card text.
  • Plugin Language – translations for the plugin’s own interface strings.

The page also includes a source locale selector. The selected source locale is saved to site_config under the key ml_source_locale.

When the form is submitted, the plugin iterates over the submitted translation fields and saves each translation using ml_set_translation().

docs.title: 7. Data Flow Example
docs.text:
A typical translation flow for the About Us section follows these steps:

  1. The homepage template calls __('about_us_content', 'index').
  2. The core __() function loads the index language file. If no static translation exists, it passes the original value through the translate filter.
  3. The Dynamic Multi-Language plugin’s first translate filter runs.
  4. It checks for a custom translation under __custom. If no match is found, it applies the siteMap and identifies that the key corresponds to the about_us site configuration field.
  5. The plugin calls ml_get_translation('site_config', 'about_us', 'config_value').
  6. ml_get_translation checks whether the current locale is the source locale. If not, it queries the ml_translations table.
  7. If a translation exists, it is returned. Otherwise, the original value is returned.
  8. The homepage displays the translated About Us content.

docs.title: 8. Plugin Uninstallation
docs.text:
The plugin registers an uninstall hook:

LabPress_Hooks::addAction('plugin_uninstalled', function($slug) {
    if ($slug === 'dynamic-multilang') {
        $db = LabPress::db();
        $db->exec("DROP TABLE IF EXISTS `ml_translations`");
    }
});

When the plugin is uninstalled, the ml_translations table is dropped. The plugin directory is then removed by the core plugin uninstall process.

Because the uninstall hook is fired before the plugin files are deleted, the plugin can safely perform cleanup operations.

docs.title: 9. Source Locale and Backend Behavior
docs.text:
The source locale is the language in which the original content is stored. By default, it is the site default language, but it can be changed through the plugin's admin page.

The plugin intentionally skips dynamic-content translation when the current request is an admin page. This ensures that administrators always see the original source content in the backend, regardless of the frontend language setting.
